client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately with my graduate program. The pressure to excel is intense, and on top of that, I’m juggling my part-time job at the coffee shop. Sometimes it feels like I'm just barely keeping my head above water, and I wonder if this whole therapy thing can even help me manage all this stress.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load right now, and it's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed. Balancing a demanding graduate program with a job can create a lot of pressure. What specific thoughts come to mind when you feel like you’re just barely keeping your head above water?

client: When I feel like I'm barely keeping my head above water, my mind races with thoughts like "I'm going to fail" or "I can't handle this." It’s like this constant loop of self-doubt that makes it hard to focus on what I need to do. I also feel a weight on my chest, which just adds to the anxiety that I might not be able to get everything done. I'm not sure how thinking differently about it would help when it feels so real and heavy right now.
therapist: It’s really tough when those self-doubting thoughts take over, and it’s completely valid to feel the physical weight of that anxiety. The feelings and thoughts you're experiencing are very real, yet they can sometimes cloud our ability to see alternative perspectives. What if we explored the evidence behind those thoughts? Are there times when you’ve successfully managed difficult tasks or overcome challenges before?

client: I guess there have been times when I’ve managed to pull through tough situations, like last semester when I was able to finish my thesis on time despite feeling overwhelmed. But even then, it felt like I was just barely scraping by, and I worry that I might not be able to replicate that success again. It’s hard to trust that I can handle it when everything feels so chaotic right now. How do I know this time will be different?
therapist: It's great to hear that you’ve experienced success in the past, even when it felt challenging. Recognizing those moments can help remind you that you have the ability to navigate tough situations. It’s understandable to worry about whether you can replicate that success, especially when things feel chaotic. What if we focused on small, manageable steps you can take right now to create a sense of control in your situation?

client: I see what you're saying about taking small steps, but I worry that even those might feel overwhelming. It’s like I’m stuck in this mindset where I can’t see past the big picture of everything I have to do. What if I try to focus on one small thing and then get sidetracked or feel anxious again? It just seems really hard to maintain that sense of control when everything feels so chaotic.
therapist: It’s completely understandable to feel hesitant about taking small steps when the bigger picture feels overwhelming. That sense of chaos can make it hard to feel in control, and it’s okay to acknowledge that. What if we brainstorm some very tiny, specific tasks that feel achievable, and we can also think about strategies to gently bring your focus back if you start to feel sidetracked? What’s one small thing you could try to tackle this week?

client: I appreciate the idea of breaking things down into tiny tasks, but I still feel a bit lost on where to even start. It’s like I can’t see anything that feels manageable right now. Maybe I could try to outline just one section of my assignment, but what if I get stuck or can’t focus? I’m worried that even that small task will just add to my anxiety instead of helping me feel more in control.
therapist: It’s completely normal to feel lost when trying to figure out where to start, especially when anxiety is involved. Outlining even one section might feel daunting, and it’s okay to acknowledge that. How about we try to set a very short time limit for that task, like just 5 or 10 minutes? This way, you can give yourself permission to stop if it starts to feel overwhelming. What do you think about trying that approach?

client: Setting a time limit does sound a bit more manageable, but I still have my doubts. What if I sit down to work for those 5 or 10 minutes and end up feeling too anxious to even get started? I worry that trying to outline might just remind me of how much I still have left to do, making it even harder to focus. It feels like I’m in this cycle where any attempt to break things down still leads me back to feeling overwhelmed.
therapist: It’s completely understandable to have doubts about starting, especially when the anxiety feels so strong and persistent. It sounds like you’re experiencing a cycle that’s tough to break, and that can be really discouraging. What if we tried to approach this differently by giving yourself permission to not get it perfect? Perhaps you could start by just jotting down any thoughts or ideas that come to mind for a few minutes, without the pressure of creating a structured outline. How does that sound to you?

client: Jotting down thoughts instead of trying to create a perfect outline does sound a bit easier, but I still can't shake the feeling that it might not be enough. What if I write something down and then feel even more confused about how to organize it later? It’s hard to let go of that pressure to be organized, especially when I feel like I have to impress my professors. I just wonder if that really will help me feel any better about the whole situation.
therapist: It's completely normal to feel pressure to impress your professors, and it’s understandable that you worry about feeling confused afterward. Letting go of the need for perfection can be challenging, especially in an academic environment. What if we reframed that experience as a way to simply get your ideas flowing without the expectation of organization? Sometimes, just expressing your thoughts can provide clarity later on. How do you think you might feel if you allowed yourself that freedom to explore your ideas without the pressure to organize them right away?

client: I can see how just letting my ideas flow could be helpful, but I still feel anxious about not having a clear structure. What if I end up writing a bunch of random thoughts that don’t really connect? It kind of feels like I’m setting myself up for more confusion later, and I’m not sure if that’s really going to help me feel any less overwhelmed. I just want to find a way to manage everything without getting stuck in my head.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel anxious about not having a clear structure, especially when you’re used to aiming for organization in your work. It’s okay to have that concern, and the fear of confusion is valid. What if you viewed this initial writing as a brainstorming session, where the goal is simply to capture thoughts without judgment? You can always revisit and organize them later. How might it feel to approach it as an experiment rather than a final product?

client: Approaching it as an experiment does take some of the pressure off, but I’m still struggling to shake the anxiety around it. I can see the value in brainstorming without judgment, but what if I write a bunch of things that don’t make sense or feel relevant later? It feels like there’s still this fear that I’ll end up wasting my time or making things even more complicated for myself.
therapist: It's completely valid to feel anxious about the possibility of writing things that might not seem relevant later, and it’s understandable to worry about wasting time. Those feelings can create a lot of pressure, especially when you're already feeling overwhelmed. What if you remind yourself that the purpose of brainstorming is to explore and generate ideas without the expectation of them all being perfect or relevant? Sometimes, even seemingly unrelated thoughts can spark connections or insights later on. How might you approach this brainstorming session with curiosity instead of judgment?

client: I get what you’re saying about approaching it with curiosity, but I still feel a bit stuck. The idea of exploring without judgment is nice in theory, but I worry that once I start writing, I might get frustrated if things don’t come together. It’s like I can’t shake this fear that I’ll just end up in a tangled mess of thoughts, and that makes me hesitant to even try. How do I find the motivation to start when I feel like I might just spiral into more anxiety?
therapist: It’s completely understandable to feel hesitant about starting when the fear of frustration and a tangled mess looms large. That fear can really hold you back, especially when you’re already feeling overwhelmed. What if we focused on giving yourself permission to write whatever comes to mind, knowing that it’s just a starting point? You could set an intention to simply explore your thoughts, and if it feels overwhelming, you can always take a break. How does that idea resonate with you?
